ety.text: From Middle English ruby, rube, from Old French rubi, from Medieval Latin rubīnus. Doublet of rubi and rubine. Etymology 1 sense 7 (“pronunciation guide”) is from the British 5½-point type size (etymology 1 sense 6), used for annotations in printed documents.

senses.d: A clear, deep, red variety of corundum, valued as a precious stone.
A deep red colour.
ex: When now I thinke you can behold such sights, / And keepe the naturall Rubie of your Cheekes, / When mine is blanch'd with feare.

senses.d: The tincture red or gules.
A ruby hummer, a South American hummingbird, Clytolaema rubricauda.
A red bird-of-paradise, Paradisaea rubra.
The size of type between pearl and nonpareil, standardized as 5½-point.
A pronunciation guide written above or beside Chinese characters.
A red spinel.
Of a deep, red color; ruby-red.
To make red; to redden.
ex: With sanguine drops the walls are rubied

ety.text: Inherited from Old French rubi, rubin, borrowed from Medieval Latin rubinus, from Latin rubeus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin rubīnus.
15th-century borrowing from Catalan robí, from Old French rubin, from Medieval Latin rubīnus, from Latin rubeus (“red”) + -īnus (diminutive).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese rubi, from Catalan robí (“ruby”), from Medieval Latin rubīnus, from Latin rubeus (“red”).

Inherited from Middle English rubben, of unknown origin; possibly ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rubbōną, related to *reufaną (“to tear”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian rubje (“to rub, scrape”), German Low German rubben (“to rub”), Low German rubblig (“rough, uneven”), Dutch robben, rubben (“to rub smooth; scrape; scrub”), Danish rubbe (“to rub, scrub”), Icelandic and Norwegian rubba (“to scrape”). More at reave. Compare typologically Latin fricō < friō < Proto-Indo-European *bʰreyH- (whence also Russian брить (britʹ, “to shave”)).

senses.d: An act of rubbing.
ex: Give that lamp a good rub and see if any genies come out.

senses.d: A difficulty or problem.
A quip or sarcastic remark.
In the game of crown green bowls, any obstacle by which a bowl is diverted from its normal course.
Any substance designed to be applied by rubbing.
ex: a heat rub intended for muscular strains

senses.d: A mixture of spices applied to meat before it is barbecued.
A loan.
To move (one object) while maintaining contact with another object over some area, with pressure and friction.
ex: I rubbed the cloth over the glass.
The cat rubbed itself against my leg.

senses.d: To be rubbed against something.
ex: My shoes are beginning to rub.

senses.d: To spread a substance thinly over; to smear.
ex: meat rubbed with spices before barbecuing
The smoothed plank, […] / New rubbed with balm.

senses.d: To move or pass with difficulty.
ex: to rub through woods, as huntsmen

senses.d: To scour; to burnish; to polish; to brighten; to cleanse; often with up or over.
ex: to rub up silver
The whole business of our redemption is, in short, only to rub over the defaced copy of the creation

senses.d: To hinder; to cross; to thwart.
ex: 'Tis the duke's pleasure, / Whose disposition, all the world well knows, / Will not be rubbed nor stopped.

senses.d: To touch the jack with the bowl.

to rub something against (a second thing)
to spread a substance thinly over; to smear

From Middle French frotter, from Old French froter (“to stroke, wipe, rub”), of uncertain origin. Generally assumed to be from Latin frictāre, frequentative of fricāre through its past participle frictus (“rubbed”).

From Lombardic *straufinōn, from Proto-Germanic *straipijaną, *stripōną (“to touch”), of uncertain ultimate origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *ster-, *strē- (“strip, streak”), see also Lithuanian strėlė (“arrow, dart, jib”), Latvian strēle (“arrow, dart”), Proto-Slavic *strěla (“arrow”).
From earlier *frecàre, from Latin fricāre.
Borrowed from French frotter.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *stricāre or Latin extricāre. Compare Sicilian stricari, Old Italian stricare, strigare; cf. also Romanian strica. Cognate with English extricate.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish ungir, borrowed from Latin ungere.

From rub + -er. The sense of the substance comes from its ability to function as an eraser, displacing earlier caoutchouc. The senses not pertaining to rubbing or erasing are secondarily derived from the name of the substance.
Unknown.

senses.d: Pliable material derived from the sap of the rubber tree; a hydrocarbon biopolymer of isoprene.
Natural rubber or any of various synthetic materials with similar properties as natural rubber.
An eraser.
ex: Stan stole a diary and some pens, pencils, ink and rubbers during his early days as a POW working on the Singapore docks.

senses.d: A condom, especially an external condom.
ex: And the rubbers you hide / In your top left pocket
My daddy said "Treat young girls like your mother" / My momma said "Trust no hoe, use a rubber"

senses.d: Someone or something which rubs.
One who rubs down horses.
One who practises massage.
ex: I curl his perriwig, paint his cheeks, perfume his breath; I am his froterer or rubber in a hot-house

senses.d: A coarse towel for rubbing the body.
An abrasive for rubbing with: a whetstone, file, or emery cloth, etc.
The cushion of an electric machine.
Not covered by funds on account.
syn: I wouldn't take a check from him. They're pure rubber.

senses.d: The entire series, of an odd number of games or matches in which ties are impossible (especially a series of three games in bridge or whist).
ex: […] an old lady's innocent rubber.
They played, and Creed and his young partner won the first rubber, winning the two first games running.

senses.d: An individual match within the series (especially in racquet sports).
ex: Ladies matches shall consist of 6 rubbers. Each rubber shall consist of best of 3 games to 21 points.
Montreal’s Francoise Abanda lost the first rubber of the tie 6-2, 6-4 to Karolina Pliskova on Saturday

senses.d: A rubber match; a game or match played to break a tie.
The game of rubber bridge.
To eavesdrop on a telephone call
To rubberneck; to observe with unseemly curiosity.
ex: Old Sally didn't talk much, except to rave about the Lunts, because she was busy rubbering and being charming.

ety.text: Borrowed from Spanish cauchuc (an early variant of caucho), from Quechua kawchu. The final -c was formerly variably pronounced or silent, but is now always silent.
Borrowed from Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi), from Egyptian qmy (“anointing oil”), qmyt (“acanthus resin, gum”).
From Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi).
Borrowed from Quechua kawchu.
Inherited from Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi).
Borrowed from Classical Nahuatl ōlli (“latex”).

ety.text: Borrowed from Spanish borracha (“wineskin”); because native Amazonians used rubber to make waterskins, the meaning began to apply to the substance.
Ultimately from Latin caput (“head”), with the diminutive French suffix -ote. Piecewise doublet of capot.
From préserver (“to preserve”) + -atif (“-ative”).
From camisa (“shirt”) + -inha (diminutive-forming suffix). The “condom” sense is a clipping of camisinha de vênus, the diminutive of camisa de vênus.

Inherited from Middle English robous (“rubbish, building rubble”), further origin uncertain; possibly from Anglo-Norman rubous, rubouse, rubbouse (“refuse, waste material; building rubble”), and compare Anglo-Latin rebbussa, robousa, robusium, robusum, rubisum, rubusa, rubusium (although the Anglo-Norman and Anglo-Latin words may be derived from the English word instead of the other way around, as there are no known Old French cognates of the word). The English word may be related to rubble, though the connection is unclear.

senses.d: Refuse, waste, garbage, junk, trash.
ex: The rubbish is collected every Thursday in Gloucester, but on Wednesdays in Cheltenham.
What traſh is Rome? / What Rubbiſh and what Offall? when it ſerues / For the baſe matter, to illuminate / So vile a thing as Cæsar.

senses.d: An item, or items, of low quality.
ex: Much of what they sell is utter rubbish.
"And ain't you had nothing but that kind of rubbage to eat?" / "No, sah—nuffn' else."

senses.d: Nonsense.
ex: Everything the teacher said during that lesson was rubbish. How can she possibly think that a bass viol and a cello are the same thing?
syn: all my eye and Betty Martin

senses.d: Debris or ruins of buildings; rubble.
ex: E'er since poor Cheapside cross in rubbage lay, […]

senses.d: Exceedingly bad; awful.
ex: This has been a rubbish day, and it’s about to get worse: my mother-in-law is coming to stay.

senses.d: Used to express that something is exceedingly bad, awful, or terrible.
ex:
- The one day I actually practice my violin, the teacher cancels the lesson.
- Aw, rubbish! Though at least this means you have time to play football.

senses.d: Used to express that what was recently said is nonsense or untrue; balderdash!, nonsense!
ex: Rubbish! I did nothing of the sort!

senses.d: To criticize, to denigrate, to denounce, to disparage.
ex: Delia's Complete Cookery Course is still in print more than 40 years since its first publication. “Everybody did rubbish it,” she says.

senses.d: To litter.

to criticize, denigrate — see also criticize, denigrate
